utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The reason why we have a late start this morning is because there was a meeting between the parties and the Presiding Judge in Chambers to see to what extent problems over the 92 ter statement of Witness Zlatkovic could be resolved. I think we -- although we start a bit later, that we may have saved a lot of time. Meanwhile, I can inform the parties that the Chamber accepts that where the parties have reached an agreement, an agreement to some extent already reached before the meeting this morning between the parties and myself. Some of the agreements even reached during the meeting. Two issues prominently remaining, that is paragraph 13 and paragraph 20. The ruling of the Chamber is that paragraph 20 is not admissible. As far as paragraph 13 is concerned, those portions on which the parties had not reached an agreement, there the Chamber admits those remaining paragraphs and annexes, with the exception -- or I should say the reservation that the Chamber would still like to pay further attention to annexes 4 and annex -- annexes 4 and 10. These are documents for -- we had not yet during the weekend the translation available so we have to read it. Annex 10 is a rather lengthy document which we would like to re-read before we finally decide whether or not to admit the paragraph in which annex 10 is presented. This is guidance for the parties. Mr. Dutertre, I take it that you will provide the Chamber with an amended -- a corrected document. Of course, if we are talking about admission, the Chamber has not yet received the attestations. So whatever I just said is of course subject to the attestations to be given by the witness. Mr. Dutertre, are you ready to call your next witness, which I do understand will be Mr. Zlatkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I will file in due course a consolidated version of the statement that could be admitted temporarily once the witness has recognised it, if you agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and has attested to it. Of course, there's no problem, I think, with attestations if only portions are taken out. Because if the witness says that whatever he said is properly reflected in the document and he would give the same answers, that of course does not preclude the Chamber from partly admitting only and the Prosecution from only partly tendering that document. Then -- I see Madam Usher has left the courtroom already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we're waiting. I briefly had a conversation with Mr. Dutertre to make sure that there - just because of the way that this witness comes to us - that there's no further Rule 68 disclosure with regard to this witness, and I have been told that there is not. I just got confirmation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as I know, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zlatkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I understand that you can hear me in a language you understand. Mr. Zlatkovic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The -- Madam Usher now hands out to you the text of the solemn declaration, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zlatkovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Dutertre, who is counsel for the Prosecution. And I take it that he has informed you already about the procedure, mainly that your written statement is already presented to the Chamber, which allows us to avoid that you have to give your whole story again but that on major parts we can read it from your statement. Mr. Dutertre, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zlatkovic. First of all, is your name Radovan Zlatkovic, you were born on the 19th of November, 1948, in Lepcince, in the municipality of Vranje and you are a retired police officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Radovan Zlatkovic, born in 1948 in Vranje, and, yes, I am a retired policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zlatkovic. Do you remember giving an interview in May and in June of last year?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, can you have a look at the binder that is to your right and tell me if that -- these documents are related to the interview you gave with the relevant annexes. In this binder, you should find the statement in your own language as well as the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When Mr. Zlatkovic views the document, on the transcript it says "last year," whereas I take it you meant to say this year, Mr. Dutertre. I don't know what you said in French; I was listening to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said last May or last June. It's a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now corrected. And I would like to express my appreciation that we only so little have to spend any time on small and quite understandable translation errors. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, do you remember this document, is this your consolidated interview -- the annexes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my consolidated interview, statement, and I do recognise it as being my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement reflect your testimony in relation to the facts that are mentioned in the statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last question on this matter. If these same questions, the questions were put to you in May and June, if these questions were put to you again today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this 104 first statements -- paragraphs of the statement. We have an index with the various annexes, and that will be consolidated as well to take into account the agreement reached by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, I have a number of questions to put to you about a number of issues. I'm going to ask you to give me very specific and concise answers. I'm going to deal with a number of issues, starting with the attack in Glodjane on the 24th of March, 1998. Please look at paragraph 23 of your statement. You state that you arrived whilst the fighting was still going on. Can you tell us roughly how long the fighting had been going on when you arrived on site in Glodjane on the 24th of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived on the 24th of March, 1998, the fighting had been going on for about an hour, two hours at the most, and I was sent there to carry an on-site investigation after the deaths -- or death of a policeman, Miodrag Otovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did the fighting start -- or last after you arrived on site?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The fighting went on until our forces withdrew, which was at around 2000 hours in the evening, because it carried on not in front of Ramush Haradinaj's house but two houses away, some 500 metres away from Ramush Haradinaj's house. There are two stone houses where the fighting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that later. You're saying that the fighting lasted until 2000 hours. At what time did you arrive in Glodjane yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I arrived at about -- well, I had breakfast at about 10.00. When I was having breakfast I heard that this policeman had been killed over the radio. I took half an hour to prepare, which means I was there in about an hour, 11.00 or 12.00 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are talking about the radios, is that the police radio or the public radio station?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the radio communication line, police communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 22, you state that there were 50 or 60 police officers who came there as a reinforcement. Can you tell us what units these police officers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, they -- first of all the policemen from Decani arrived to help out, to help the police patrol, which happened to be there when Otovic was killed. Then the Djakovica police arrived, and when nothing else was done the MUP specials arrived but they were not deployed in that fighting because it grew dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What role did these special units play then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The special unit was an anti-terrorist unit, which was supposed to capture the perpetrators of this crime, but as it grew dark the unit was not deployed because it was dark and they couldn't be deployed because there would have been even more casualties. There were quite a few casualties on our side already, so actually the unit was not deployed and they were ordered to withdraw to Djakovica and they went off towards Belgrade and Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, it's not entirely clear to me. Mr. Zlatkovic, could you please repeat at what time did you withdraw in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime around 2000 hours, that's when we withdrew. It might have been 2030 hours or perhaps 2100 hours, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, you have just stated that you had a number of casualties in your ranks. Can you give us a figure, an approximate figure, of the number of people who were injured amongst you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Otovic was killed, the commander of the police department in Rznic or squad; and three or four policemen were wounded, I can't remember exactly, I think there were three or four of them. I know that there were policemen who were wounded and, as I say, three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand that Mr. Otovic and the chief of the Irzniq police was killed; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of police, the head of the department, Mr. Otovic, was in Rznic, and he was killed on the road itself, in front of Ramush's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. So it's the one and the same person, Mr. Otovic and the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: He was killed, and there were three or four policemen who were wounded during combat. And there were two young men who were terrorists with weapons, and they were killed, and they were Ramush's men. And I even think that one of them might have been related to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of weapons were used by the Serb police that came there as a reinforcement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the Serb police force who came as reinforcements used rifles, semi-automatic and automatic rifles. They didn't have any other weapons, and hand-grenades, of course, they did have those and that's what was used on both sides over there by those stone houses where this conflict came about. After -- in front of Ramush's house, when they moved on to the other two houses, both sides over there used hand-grenades, and I think that Mr. Ramush was wounded on that occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just mentioned two other houses. Can you describe these houses in which the fighters from the other side had gone?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The houses were the old-fashioned type of house, built of stone, and they were about 500 to 700 metres away from Ramush's house. They had been built -- well, quite a long time ago, built of strong stone blocks and - how shall I put this? - they had some openings, apertures on the side which were used -- I wasn't there myself but I was told by my colleagues that those openings were used by Ramush's men as points from which they could fire from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who told you that, what colleagues told you that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Zoran, he took part in that. He was born in Pec, he's a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I think his surname was Djordjevic, Zoran Djordjevic, and he was the commander of a squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At that time, how far away were you from these two houses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- well, I carried out the on-site investigation in the yard of Ramush Haradinaj's house, along the road, where Otovic was found, Milorad [as interpreted] Otovic. And then we took shelter in the house opposite -- right by the road. Mr. Ramush, I'm sure, knows whose house that was. It's right opposite his own house at a distance of maybe 150 metres. And we were in that yard, and we were sheltered because it has high walls, concrete walls, maybe from concrete blocks and there was some straw, some hay, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So when you were in that house, how far away were you from the two stone houses you've just described for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: 500 metres. The distance is the same from Ramush's house and this house and -- it's the same distance, 5 to 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Why did you take shelter in that particular house, can you give us an explanation about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we took refuge there in the yard of the house, not in the house, and we were in the yard because there was shooting from all sides. There was shooting coming from other Albanian houses, too, shooting at the members of the police force. So we took shelter to protect ourselves from the in-coming bullets because the ammunition that was used was the type that explodes in the air. Mostly it was that kind of ammunition, the projectiles explode in midair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How do you know that these were explosive bullets, did you see them yourself, with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them myself when they exploded in midair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Can you tell us about the frequency of firing. Are we talking about continuous fire or sporadic fire? Can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, there was sporadic shooting, but while we were on the spot investigating at Ramush's house, then they started throwing hand-grenades, and you could hear that. And my colleagues later on told me that Ramush's men would throw the hand-grenades behind the walls because both houses were surrounded on all sides. So they threw these hand-grenades, and our people retaliated, of course, across -- over the walls, and that's how the policemen were wounded, in this general melee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, the shooting did not just come from the two houses you've described but also from other houses. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the shooting also came from other houses, more intensive firing. As it fell dark, more intensive firing came from other houses, which means that the population was armed, perhaps not the entire population of those villages, but there were armed individuals who took the opportunity. They made use of the conflict between Mr. Ramush and the police to open fire, in order to assist Ramush and get the police to withdraw, which is what we did in order to avoid more bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You personally, had you found yourself in a situation where there was so much resistance in your previous police activity?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Not before that time, but later on I did, yes, on more than one occasion. I was attacked by terrorist groups when going to carry out on-site investigations, and I will explain where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get back to this later, indeed. In your view, Mr. Zlatkovic, the resistance against the police force, could that be improvised?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question in the sense that it's asking, as I understand it, for an expression of opinion without a foundation having been laid at this stage. And the word "improvised" in itself is a word that lacks precision. I think if Mr. Dutertre is seeking to elicit is whether there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, how would you describe the degree of organisation, of coordination, of the -- of your opponents on that day in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I was like. It was certainly not improvised. A conflict broke out for the following reasons. A few days before that, individual Roma arrived and even some Albanians and Serbs to complain that they were being ambushed by armed groups on the roads at night and mistreated. Among them, a few days before that, a young man had been caught. I cannot recall his name now, but I think his father was a taxi-driver. He was the son of Ali Baraba and Mr. Ramush probably knows the man and he knows the young man. The young man was caught, and when interviewed in Decani he said that this was being done by Mr. Haradinaj, Ramush's group, that he had engaged a group which was mistreating Serbs, disobedient Albanians and Roma, in order to drive them out of the village. When my colleagues from the state security received this information and this young man, who was Ali Baraba's son took part in that, the police started surveillance over the inhabitants of that village. There were several Serb houses in Dubrava, several in Gornje Ratiste and several in Donje Ratiste, and there were Serb houses in those villages. So the patrol was told to watch over those people, to see if they had problems. On that day, they set out. Milorad [as interpreted] Otovic, as the commander, and another policeman -- in fact, there was several policemen. When they got to the house, not right in front of the house but on the road to the house opposite Ramush Haradinaj's house, there was a young man there and another man. They wanted to start a conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, in view of the ruling of the Chamber on paragraph 20, you're invited to fully explore the source of knowledge in every detail in relation to what the witness just testified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they got to the -- a point near Ramush Haradinaj's house, there's a road --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I'd like to go one step back and to proceed methodically. How did you have any knowledge about the statements made by Ali Baraba's sons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Ali Baraba's son said that, and I held his statement in my hand -- in my hands. Later on it was used to find terrorists. It was handed to me, and I read it because I was dealing with terrorism in that secretariat. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is the person providing you with the statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I received the statement from the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When did you -- when you had this statement in your hands, did you see whether it was signed or not by Mr. Ali Baraba's son, of course?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was signed, and that young man was in detention, he was in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to my initial question. I'd asked you what the degree of organisation was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I asked you to fully explore in relation to what the witness testified. I remember that the witness testified what happened on the road before Mr. Haradinaj's house, but the source of knowledge for that has not yet been established. And apart from that, the houses, what is Mr. Haradinaj's, what is the house of others nearby where the police sought -- sought to -- refuge, to protect themselves against gun-fire. What are the houses from which shooting took place, the old stone houses? It's not entirely clear to the Chamber, also in relation to the report that appears as I think annex 12 and which, as far as I remember, I've seen that before, so that might be already in evidence. Could you try to establish that as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- might I just be heard in respect of the testimony that's been given concerning the interview with Ali Baraba's son. Simply this: It's unclear to me at this stage in the light of the answers that have been given whether this is evidence that the Prosecution is seeking to rely upon to go into the truth of its contents; but if so, it involves tendering the contents of the statement, despite the fact that the person to whom the statement was made is not identified as a witness. So I wonder if Mr. Dutertre may clarify that. If it's simply being tendered as part of a process of investigation, then that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Initially I wanted to know how well the opponents were organised. The witness answered in an -- and in so doing he spoke about Mr. Ali Baraba's son so I did take due note that there was a decision by the Trial Chamber in this respect. I did not plan to explore this particularly. I wanted to focus, rather, indeed on the actual fighting, but I could, of course, deal with your questions more specifically, asking questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, what Mr. Emmerson would like to know is whether you used this information, that is, the arrest and the statements, which I think we don't have on paper, received from the state security by yourself. If this is introduced as the reasons why surveillance and patrolling was intensified, that's a different matter than to use this information as evidence of the truth of what was stated in those statements, that is -- I don't know exactly -- of course I know what is in paragraph 20 but I have to check now the transcript. For example, whether you wanted to use this as evidence, and I'm now quoting from page 12, lines 19: "He said that this was being done by Mr. Haradinaj, Ramush's group, that he had engaged a group which was mistreating Serbs." I mean, if you want to -- I think that's -- Mr. Emmerson's question is whether you want to prove this, these activities were undertaken by a group formed by Mr. Haradinaj, or whether you just want to introduce this information, this reporting to the witness, as the reasons why they went there, intensified patrolling, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only to know why they intensified the patrol -- patrolling activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see, Mr. Emmerson, you are nodding yes. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, regarding the conditions or the circumstances of Mr. Otovic's death when he arrived to Glodjane, where do you have this information from? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived on the spot, I found Otovic lying dead on the road. We recorded that in the record of the on-site investigation. A record was drawn-up, photo documentation was adduced, and I saw this myself. I saw the man lying dead only the road with his rifle underneath him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And where was he in relation to Ramush Haradinaj's house?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: On the road some 20 or 25 metres away, maybe a little more. It's been nine years since then, and also I was not a local man. So I can't be very precise, but it was on the road in front of Ramush Haradinaj's house, maybe 50 or a hundred metres away or less, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 22, there you say that police officers, including Mr. Otovic, wanted to put questions to Mr. Haradinaj's father about his sons, and once they were in Glodjane they approached a group of people to ask about the location of Mr. Haradinaj's father's house. And you say that a young man ran towards the house and that immediately after that, fire was opened from that house. And the police asked for backup. How are you aware of these details?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived on the spot to carry out an investigation, we used the people who were there as witnesses even though they were officials. So we asked the policemen who was -- who were present what happened. Among these policemen, there was some who said that they had arrived in a vehicle, stopped on the road in front of the house because they saw a group of people standing there. Among them was a youngish man, 25, 26 years old, perhaps, and when they approached to inquire, this man started running towards Ramush Haradinaj's house and the other ones started running in the opposite direction. And Momcilo Stijovic ran after him and caught the man, and it turned out that the man was the president of the LDK. The young man who was running towards Ramush Haradinaj's house, it turned out that that was allegedly the brother of Mr. Ramush Haradinaj, Daut. Whether he really was Daut or not, we never established. But then fire was opened from the house and Otovic -- Miodrag Otovic was hit on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Agreed. Could you give us the names of the policemen who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the houses of which you said that there were a number of people firing from the houses, to be more specific as to the location. How many houses are we talking about when you said that there was firing from houses, and that's the reason you said why you sought shelter in the courtyard of the dwelling, the house, that was opposite Mr. Haradinaj's father's house?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The attack started from the house of the father of Mr. Ramush Haradinaj, Mr. Hilmi Haradinaj. A group of about 40 men ran to those two houses which were in the village but near the edge of the village, some 500 metres away. I don't know exactly whose houses those were. We couldn't establish that because we couldn't come close. Only the policemen fighting there were there. The investigating judge and I, as the inspector for terrorism and the technicians working with me, carried out an on-site investigation only on the spot where Otovic was killed, where the fighting took place, and that was Mr. Hilmi Haradinaj's house where we found a large quantity of grenades, automatic machine-guns, empty -- spent shell-casings. That's the area we covered, and we carried out an on-site investigation with Mr. Veselin Cadzanovic, an investigating judge from Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's speak about the spent shell-casings. What did you do with them, did you collect them? Did you leave them on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep interrupting. Before Mr. Dutertre moves on, the witness at line 10 and onwards on page 18 has given a lengthy account of how this incident is said to have begun of a group of 40 men running to certain houses some distance away. Again, we have to no evidence at all as to the basis for that information, unless the witness is claiming that he was present at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dutertre, apart from what Mr. Emmerson said, I can't say that matters become clearer to me. Which house belongs to whom? I mean, if I'm talking about house A or B, I'd rather know what house it is than to whom it belongs. I do understand that Mr. Otovic, that's at least the gist of the testimony, went to the house of Mr. Ramush Haradinaj; that he was killed in front of that house, being on the road. But where these other houses are located and where the attack started and what is considered to be the attack, was that the attack on Mr. Otovic, was that -- it's -- could we approach it in a more systematic way, and I'm now speaking for myself, for me photographs of the village and the nearby area has always very much helped me to understand the situation. And these photographs are already in evidence, so you could even invite the witness to mark them when he talks about the house of Hilmi, which house he exactly has in mind. I also know that some of the photographs depict rather how the situation is now compared to how it used to be, but could you try to bring me to the right houses; and, of course, also lay a foundation as far as the knowledge of the witness is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President. It's a matter of time. I have a lot of subjects to deal with. Of course, I can go into detail, but if I do so I can't sort of tackle other questions in depth. So I'll make sure that we see an aerial photograph of Glodjane for it to be more specific, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: But before we do so, Mr. Zlatkovic, tell me, could you tell us in relation to the house in front of which Mr. Otovic was killed, you sought refuge opposite that house. You said there was firing from other houses. Where were those other houses located in relation to the house in front of which Mr. Otovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Those houses were on the eastern side of the house of Mr. Haradinaj and on the north side towards Decani, or rather, that's west towards Decani. But shots did not come from the direction of Dubrava, Babaloc, and so on, but from Rznic, onwards, there was shooting from every side but that was later on when it was already dark. I was some 500 metres away from those two houses where the fighting took place, and I observed that myself. I could see fighting going on there, but to whom the houses belonged, I really don't know from whose houses they were shooting and whose houses they were surrounded. Otovic was killed and the fighting began in front of Ramush Haradinaj's house, or rather, from Ramush Haradinaj's house, and that's where he was killed. Just a minute, please. Mr. Ramush must know, it's a house --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, let's go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show on the screen Exhibit D35. This is an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And I shall ask you to mark various locations, the locations you have spoken about. You're going to see it in your screen in a few seconds. Mr. Witness -- Mr. Zlatkovic, now you can see this photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but these are new houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the village in question? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's Rznic, judging by this here, I think it's Rznic. This is all new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, would it not be most logical where the story starts at Mr. Haradinaj's house, to perhaps see whether there's any picture where Mr. Haradinaj's house would be on it? Or do you consider this to be a picture where Mr. Haradinaj's house is on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I -- well, I'm trying to find the reference. In the meantime can we move to another topic in order not to waste any time. I will come back to this later, if you so please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, you testified that in the house opposite of which Mr. Otovic had been found, you had found a number of weapons, ammunition, and spent shell-casings. What did you do with all this? More specifically, what did you do with the spent shell-casings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The spent shell-casings were gathered up by the forensic technicians and delivered to the institute for ballistic forensics in Pristina. We received information because we also collected some weapons that we found there, and it was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, as I think Mr. Dutertre knows, there is an objection which has been the subject of agreement about the witness testifying to his recollection of what the product of reports he doesn't produce said. This is the second half of the original paragraph 24 of the consolidated witness statement which has been removed by agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so. You're quite right, but you know when I put a question I can't control his answer. This was not the meaning of my question. I was not interested in the product of the report, so I have received my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Before we are able to find better photographs of the houses and the village, we'll come back to this, I'd like to move to another topic. Mr. Zlatkovic, who's Isuf Hoxha?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Isuf Hoxha is an Albanian. He was a fairly poor man and lived on some farm over there, but as we say in the Balkans he liked to have both fingers in the pie. He lived -- he was on good terms with the Serbs and on good terms with the Albanians, too. And if you want me to make this more vivid for you, he had a photograph of Slobodan Milosevic in his house and Shote Galica the Albanian hero and they were framed in one frame. So when the Albanians -- when some Albanians came by and knocked on the door he would turn the picture around to face the Albanian heroine, Shote Galica. When the Serbs came visiting he would turn the picture around to the side where there was the photograph of Slobodan Milosevic. So he was on very good terms with both sides and collaborated with the police a little as well, and that's the kind of man he was. He is divorced. His wife lives, I think, somewhere in Belgium, I think, and he was living with some of his children at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Now how come you knew about this, about this picture with photographs on either side? How come you are aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: He came to see me in my office. We talked. I talked to him personally, and he himself said that that's the kind of man he was and he lived that way, had been living that way for a long time. And as he was poor, he helped the police out and we would take him a little coffee and sugar, and he was the one who showed me the picture himself. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did he show it to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: In his house on the wall, that's where the picture -- the photograph was displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I see. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: It happened before he was kidnapped. I think it might have been May when we visited him, yes, in May, and it was in June or July when he was kidnapped between Prizren and Suva Reka. That's the information I received from his son, that that's where he was kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: No, what I meant was this: When did you have this conversation with him? When did he show you this picture frame?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: In May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: 1998. He died sometime in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said that he would help the police. What did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that he helped out the police in this area, but when it came to theft or things like that, then he moved among the local criminals. I'm not speaking about major crime, just petty crime and where young boys would steal cars, bicycles, break windows, so he helped out. He was sometimes involved in things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to another part of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, let me try to understand fully the last answer given. "What I wanted to say," the witness said, "was that he helped out the police in this area, but when it came to theft or things like that, then he moved among the local criminals." Now, what exactly did he help you out with? Would he report thefts committed by others or would he report other matters to you, such as activities of armed groups or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He helped out with the theft side of it. He was a petty criminal himself, but when it came to theft and the criminals usually used that money to gamble, and he was a gambler himself, and then he would tell us, Last night so-and-so gambled and lost so much money and then the police always had reason to believe that the money had came from some kind of theft but he didn't understand much about police matters. But he was also a member of the socialist party, let me tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- so he was not in any way assisting the police in discovering any other kind of activity, that is, not ordinary small criminality, but other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we could get further amplification with regard to page 23, line 22, the answer that's given there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you could ask that in cross-examination, Mr. Guy-Smith. Could you, therefore, confirm that he was only assisting in these, as you called it, these small theft matters and not in other matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to other matters, no, but the Albanians couldn't forgive him for being a member of the socialist party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's your interpretation. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me deal with paragraph 13, subparagraph 4, which deals with the kidnapping of Mr. Rade Popadic. Here's my question: Did you personally carry out any investigation on this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic were policemen. One was from Bogotic, the other was from Sabac, but they were in the same unit. And on that day when they were kidnapped they were going to get some food. They were on their way to Djakovica. Their vehicle broke down, they arrived at Babaloc --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rade Popadic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, could you please, the interpreters couldn't hear you. I take it that your microphone was not activated. Could you please repeat your question therefore so that it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I wanted to know simply, and we were going step by step, whether you did personally take part in the investigation on Mr. Popadic and his colleague Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally took part in the investigation of Rade -- the late Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic, and I arrived at the following information. At the time they were working in Junik, and as they were out of food they went to Djakovica --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just step by step, Mr. Zlatkovic. You said that they were kidnapped around 10.30, and you explained why or how you knew that it was around 10.30, but you say it happened at the intersection of Rastavica. How did you learn that they were kidnapped in Rastavica or what is your foundation to claim this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I say that they were kidnapped at 10.30 because they set out two or three minutes from Babaloc -- two or three minutes before 10.30 from Babaloc, from the refugee camp or settlement in Babaloc to Rastavica, and you can do that distance in two or three minutes. It takes you two or three minutes to get there, and they were kidnapped at Rastavica. Later on, I received information about the way in which this happened. Allegedly, the terrorists threw some salt on the road, on the surface of the road, and herded the sheep over the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... step by step. On what basis do you know that the kidnapping took place in Rastavica? What is the information you have that led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I drew this conclusion on the basis of some statements made by Albanians, what Albanians said when I interviewed them, not only me but my colleagues as well. And that's how we reached this conclusion, that the kidnapping had taken place exactly at that spot, at the junction at Rastavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry, before Mr. Dutertre continues, the same questions arises. We don't have these witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Zlatkovic -- Mr. Zlatkovic, we have seen a rather short report of the 26th of May, at least the Chamber is reading this and considering whether it should be admitted into evidence. Now that only very briefly describes without a lot of details that these two police officers were kidnapped and that at least they changed car because they set off in a Kadett and later on continued driving a Mitsubishi. Now, when you talk about these statements given by Albanians, were they put on paper? When were they given? To whom were they given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statements were recorded and given to the state security staff, and I used them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they still available? Because we have seen some of these reports. Do they still exist, these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain they do within the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, have you tried to -- I mean, if there are detailed statements about how this all happened, including details as salt on the road and sheep licking the salt and thus obstructing the passage of cars, that would give at least more details than we find in the annex 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President. I did provide in the annex the information I had, and it seems as though there is more information, as is stated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate my objection goes rather deeper in the sense, again, the question I'm putting is whether or not this -- the contents of these accounts are being tendered as evidence of the truth of their contents, because if they are then frankly the right course would be to identify the witnesses and have them as part of the Prosecution case so they can be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, it seems that Mr. Emmerson would not insist on receiving the other statements if you don't use them, or at least if you don't use this hearsay evidence as evidence which could establish the truth of -- well, let's say the story with -- about the abduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not have such statements here and now, but the witness himself carried out the investigation, he said, and today in this courtroom this is the best evidence I have to give you. So this is a matter of weight which will have to be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the witness says there's better evidence, but the question is not whether this is the best evidence, yes or no, but whether you introduce this evidence as -- for the purposes of establishing what happened to the two police officers or for other reasons, such as tension at that time in the area in May. I mean, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Mr. President. This is to establish what really happened with regard to these two police officers, and we are of the view that this information, such as it is, is such that it can help -- help the Judges have a better idea as to the truth with relation to these two police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness might be asked to remove his headphones at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's first ask. Mr. Zlatkovic, do you understand any English? Let's move in a different way. Mr. Zlatkovic, we are at a time when we need --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at a time when we need a break anyhow, and since the parties would like to exchange some views on procedural matters, perhaps I already give you an opportunity to start the break now. Madam Usher, could you -- we'll have a break of approximately a half an hour, Mr. Zlatkovic, and we'd like to see you back after the break. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Zlatkovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, when you tell us that you want to use this evidence in order to give -- to assist the Chamber in getting to the truth, the issue is what truth are you actually trying to establish. I notice that the kidnapping, as it is said, of these police officers are not incidents which are specifically mentioned in the indictment; to that extent, it -- one could wonder why it is important to know who exactly and in what way kidnapped these two persons. Another way of establishing the truth is to say, Well, what happened in these times is that people disappeared, and perhaps it is not without importance that it -- here there were two police officers that disappeared on that-and-that day, as it was reported to us, rather than to emphasise who had done it, whether it was with sheep or without sheep. And I think that that's what's bothering Mr. Emmerson mainly. Mr. Emmerson, is that more or less --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The concern --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point, Mr. President. Mr. Rade Popadic was identified as being the body R-31. So this is the reason why we wanted to expand on his case and know more about the circumstances of his disappearance. If he has been somebody not listed in the indictment, quite rightly so, Mr. President, we'd just have made sure the date was mentioned. But he happens to be under Count -- Counts 21 and 22, and I'd like to seek as much evidence as possible from this witness, who carried out the investigations, even if we do not have all the reports he refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I respond briefly. R-31 has been DNA identified as Rade Popadic. The evidence that the Prosecution proposes to adduce provides no account as to the circumstances of his death at all, other than the fact that his wife is in a position to identify when it was she last saw him and his commanding officer, who is a witness that the Prosecution does propose to call, can give evidence as to the instructions that he was given when he left to -- left Junik and was due to return and spoke to him by telephone from Babaloc. That witness is called Rade Ripic. As far as I understand, there's been no suggestion that there's a protective measures application in respect of him. I see -- before I go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. I must admit that I overlooked paragraph 79 of the -- at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But the concern I have is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- if the evidence that is currently being elicited is elicited with a view to assisting the Trial Chamber to understand what happened to an armed police officer and how he met his death, then hearing from this witness third-hand accounts from individuals that he claims to have interviewed where we don't have the witness statement, we have no means of knowing whether the individuals themselves were recounting things they had seen or things they'd heard or who had told them, and where we have seen in other instances already in this case, accounts recorded in witness statements taken allegedly at Gjakove police station, which are then disavowed for reasons explained by the persons who are supposed to have made them, for the Prosecution at this stage to be seeking to prove the circumstances in which these two individuals met their deaths, if indeed the second one is dead because there's no evidence of the recovery of remains in respect of the other police officer, through evidence of this quality, in our submission, is objectionable. It doesn't assist the Trial Chamber. I'm not making a bland hearsay objection; we're simply not in a position to test it. I mean, the right way -- if the Prosecution wants to put this as part of its case the right way would be to identify the people concerned and to call them as witnesses so they can be cross-examined. Not to seek to do the very thing that the Prosecution has done or attempted to do now on a number of occasions which, in the event, they've each time backed down; namely, to get an investigator to try to tell the Trial Chamber what someone they've interviewed would have said if they'd been a witness in the case. It's not a proper way to proceed, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note of the submissions of the Defence. Nevertheless, this is some kind of evidence with regard to what happened. We've had statements taken by this witness with various individuals, and I keep thinking that the matter is -- is a matter of weight rather than admissibility. And today, this is the best evidence available regarding this event in addition to the two statements made by the wife of one of the two police officers and Mr. Ripic, the superior of the two police officers. Now, of course, I do agree it is up for the Trial Chamber to assess the weight to give to this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is seeking to enter this evidence for the truth of the matter asserted. There is -- as Mr. Emmerson said, there is no way for this evidence to be tested. This is the precise difficulty that we were having earlier when we were dealing with this particular paragraph and the subparagraphs, paragraph 13. It is inadmissible under the Rules of Evidence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the position of Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Dutertre, I noticed that you had been present during all these interviews. I just put a question to the witness about whether he -- whether he did put on paper or whether the statement of those who reported the events, that is, how this person and when and where he was kidnapped, whether this was put on paper. The witness says, Yes. Did you ever put that question to the witness when preparing for his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was implicit when we had the statement, but the question as such was not put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did you try to obtain these statements of those who were at the source of -- of these findings or this -- rather, these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to look at our RFAs to know about that more exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the witness already in his report gives quite some details as -- for example, as to where exactly these people were kidnapped in annex 4, which is dated the 26th of May, where the events are supposed to have taken place on the 24th. So therefore, you would expect at least that this information to be made available in two days. The Chamber will further consider the matter to what extent it will --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I have one further sentence in relation to this because it does seem to be a recurring problem and it came into focus during the evidence of the investigator Pekka Haverinen. At one point it looked as though the Prosecution was seeking, through the evidence of a witness testifying about photo-boards, to elicit in substance the testimony which is recorded in the statements to which the photo-boards related. And I can -- Your Honours will recall at the time excited some anxiety on the part of the Defence, that what the Prosecution was effectively assuming was that there was a permissible mechanism for adducing evidence before this Tribunal whereby direct evidence of witnesses whose testimony would go to the acts and conduct of the accused can be called not by putting a witness in the witness box but simply by calling the person who took their statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not talking about "simply," Mr. Emmerson; matters are more complicated. This annex 4 at least establishes that by whatever means on the 26th of May, that there was knowledge or a presumption on what happened with some details, which may have some probative value, either against or in favour of the accused. So therefore, the -- I do understand the concern of the Defence expressed repeatedly, that by just giving a rather vague report that the Chamber should not admit that or use that as to establish what is in that report. At the same time, if you say it's not admissible evidence, then you could use it in no way. And as you may be aware, the Chamber will, very cautiously, see how to evaluate the evidence, including such reports as this one, and as I said several times before, if someone writes down, I heard from Mr. A, B, and C, of which I do not remember the name, that five persons were killed by accused Q, Y, or Z on the 25th of March, 1998, the Chamber will not use that as accepting that this is what happened. At the same time, such a report, for example, could establish that at a certain moment those who wrote that report lived in the assumption that people were killed or at least not alive anymore. So therefore, evaluation --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't for a second seek to go behind the summary that Your Honour has just put to me, indeed, I wouldn't quarrel with it for a moment. The distinction, though, is between whether the document is tendered as to the truth of its contents or not. Because plainly if it's tendered to show the state of mind of the person writing it, that is one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then of course, if we later hear six witnesses who in person testify that they gave a statement at that time to the police in which they said so and so and so, then of course the documents could confirm that. And if a witness at any moment would change his statement, then the mere fact that at that time they gave a statement could be used with all caution to either choose from the one version or the other version. So to that extent there is no one full hundred per cent of saying it's excluded forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I wasn't really -- just to make it absolutely clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- that the purpose of my submission at this stage was not to press upon the Trial Chamber an application to exclude annex 4. The purpose of my submission was, as I thought I'd indicated right at the outset, to seek clarification about whether the account that's being elicited from this witness is being tendered to show the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If the answer to that is no, I'll sit down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. And if the answer is yes, then that still doesn't mean that the Chamber would adopt the same view when evaluating his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so the Chamber is clear about my position, my concern is once again if the document is being offered for the truth of the matter asserted then my concern is being voiced as being something that presently is inadmissible. I understand the Chamber's analysis and I once again -- I don't disagree with that either. The difficulty that I'm having at the present time is precisely that the concerns that have been voiced by Mr. Emmerson at present and was voiced previously, which it seems is it what is occurring here is the Prosecution is seeking to introduce evidence in an impermissible fashion to establish the truth of the contents or the truth of the assertion and therein lies the rub. And if they're doing it for some other purpose, then I too will not rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether the intention of the party presenting the evidence is decisive or whether the interpretation of the Chamber receiving the evidence is decisive is, however, another matter. Mr. Dutertre, would you like to add anything before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that we want to offer this document in order to establish and to prove what happened to these two police officers. It's a relevant document. It has a degree of probative value, and hearsay evidence is not inadmissible before this Tribunal. It's up to the Judges to give the appropriate weight to the exhibit. Hearsay is perfectly acceptable in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises to the parties to the late restart, at the same time the Chamber hopes that the parties rest assured that there are usually rather urgent matters that keep us out of court. Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed, and the objections received in distinct ways so as not to admit or not to exclude or -- are not ignored by the Chamber, but the Chamber allows you to continue as you did before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will be rather brief. I've already used up all the time allocated to me. I will deal with four issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zlatkovic, I will ask you to give me very concise answers. Page 25, line 10 of your testimony today on the transcript you say: [In English] "With regard to other matters, no, but the Albanians could not forgive for being a member of the socialist party." [Interpretation] Could you give us the name of the socialist party you're referring to, the entire name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what you mean by that the Albanians could not forgive him, what do you mean by that? What could they not forgive him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't forgive him that because the Albanians had already established the VSK party, under the leadership of the late Mr. Rugova, so they had a party of their own through which they fought for their alleged rights. But this man was on the side of the socialist party, that's why, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, they couldn't forgive him -- I mean, I do understand that this is an explanation you consider to be a likely explanation. Could you give us any more details about -- did anyone tell you this or is it just your interpretation of what you observed or -- it's not clear if you say the Albanians could not forgive him, that, if you take it literally, would mean all Albanians being aware and not willing to forgive. Could you give us some more details or to tell us whether it's just your impression of what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give some more details about this. I heard this from his son. When he was kidnapped between Prizren and Suva Reka, when the Hoxha set out towards Suva Reka to gamble --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Hoxha, not the Hoxha, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a group of Albanians came along which searched the bus looking for Serbs among them. Hoxha was there, and while they were looking at personal identity papers he threw away his membership card of the Socialist Party of Serbia through the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this what the son told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, his son told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was his son present when it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether his son heard it from someone else or whether he was present, but he came to report his father as missing. When Hoxha was on his way back, when the Albanians got out, the terrorist group, when they left the bus, they found the membership card, Hoxha's membership card in the socialist party. His name was on it. On the following day or a few days later, they ambushed him again, they found him, and then they kidnapped him. But I really don't know how his son learned this, but his son personally told me about this when he came to report his father missing, and then he talked to me on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me go back to the Glodjane incident, paragraph 23 of your statement you state that you arrived on site, that the fighting had already started, and that the police officers on site told you that there were around 40 armed men who had left Mr. Haradinaj's house. Based on your experience of the events on that particular day and based of what you saw of the fighting, what is your estimate about the number of fighters on Mr. Haradinaj's side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day there were about 40 men, about 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And when you give us this figure, it's based on what you saw yourself or on the fierceness of the fighting? How do you come to this figure of 40 people?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I base this figure on what the policemen told me when they were -- when the policemen were going forward, they withdrew towards the houses. And in late February, when one policeman from the neighbouring village Dubrava, Dragan Stojanovic was a neighbor of Mr. Haradinaj's, was out hunting. He found a round, an empty round, in the Biteska forest, and I was ordered by my supervisor to take a group of policemen and to search that forest. In the forest I found three fires burning in different places, about eight or ten empty cases for ammunition. Then I found empty tins of where they had had fish and I found old boots, and I found cigarette butts. And then I wrote a report and said that 30 or 40 men had been in that forest, and then a few days later this tragic murder happened and the conflict with Ramush Haradinaj's group. And about 40 men came out of his house, maybe not all of them were fighters. Maybe Mr. Hilmi Haradinaj was among them, he was an elderly man at the time. Maybe there were children among them, but about 40 people left the house of Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This is what the police officers told you. I'd like you to be shown 65 ter Exhibit 1766. It's an aerial photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet in evidence, Mr. Dutertre, I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not yet in evidence. Scroll down a bit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, do you recognise the place that is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You have a marker, and the usher may be able to help you in this, could you please mark on this photograph the location of the house of the Haradinaj family?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, we have talked about Ramush Haradinaj's house, the family house, I think his father's house. Could you just ask the witness to mark whatever he recognises on this village -- on this photograph and then tell us whether that is a house which he described as one of the Haradinaj houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, we see a house in -- on the -- in the lower parts of this photograph. Do you recognise this house?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: There were several unfinished houses in that area. They hadn't been whitewashed on the outside. They hadn't been plastered. If this is the road leading through Dubrava, then this house would be Ramush Haradinaj's house, and this is the house where we took shelter. But I think it doesn't have a roof now, the one up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we invite the witness to mark it as such because I do not see -- no, I don't see anything at this moment on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was about to ask him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, can you please mark these locations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, you've marked things on this photograph before we've asked you anything. What have you marked with the figure number "1" on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I marked what I assume is Ramush Haradinaj's house at the time, but -- and this is the house we took shelter in while the fighting was going on up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is it the house you marked with "2"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Number "2", but I don't see a roof on it now. I see just the wall, but that's what it was like more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, again, I think the witness testified there were two houses they took refuge. Could you ask the witness to identify, if it's on the photograph, the other house they used to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the houses where the fighters on the side of Mr. Haradinaj's took shelter or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, would you please mark on the photograph the location of the second house where you took shelter on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 2, if that's the road. There were some other houses at the time which were not finished, but if this was taken after the war, it doesn't correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In how many houses did you take refuge on that day, one house? Two houses? Three houses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: In one house. We took shelter in one house, and next to the house was the anti-terrorist unit which arrived. It was -- it was near the house, but it didn't look like this then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last question. Would you be able to mark on this photograph the two stone houses where you said that the people who left Mr. Haradinaj's house then went and took shelter? Can you please write the following numbers: 3 and 4 on these two houses if you find them.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see them, but they're somewhere around here, around here. But I don't see that clearly on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this photograph, and I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P818, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection against admission? I don't hear any objection, then it is admitted into evidence. Please proceed. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Emmerson, who is counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, can we start, please, by looking at your witness statement that you have in front of you at paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: If it can assist --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said; the interpreter did not hear clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, you earlier said something the interpreters could not hear. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I need help to find paragraph 28, but now I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you some questions about a number of paragraphs in your statement, and as you can see each one has a separate number. So I want to start please with paragraph 28 and with the first sentence in that paragraph. Does it read as follows: "From the 24th of March, 1998, when Miodrag Otovic was killed, until September 1998, the police never returned to Glodjane"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you turn to paragraph 31, please, where you describe in the paragraph 31 and the paragraphs which follow two occasions when there were, you say, attempts by the MUP to enter the territory on the eastern side of the main Peje to Gjakove road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: It's true that the MUP tried to enter on the 2nd of August, 1998, in order to get a terrorist group out and free up the communication, that the Serbs in Djakovica and the other population that were not involved in terrorist activities were using to get supplies of food and other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there. You describe in paragraph 31 an attempt that was made by the MUP on the 2nd of August, and in paragraph 33 a second operation conducted on the 9th of August. Do you see those two operations described?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the first one at paragraph 31 you say at the bottom of that paragraph, last few lines, you say that: "The MUP could reach the junction between the main road," the Gjakove-Decan road, "and the Prilep road." And you say a little further on: "As the terrorists were numerous and well organised, the MUP had to withdraw." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The MUP had to withdraw because they had losses on their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So is it your evidence then that on that 2nd of August attempt, the MUP did not succeed in penetrating at all into the territory to the east of the main road?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Neither to the east nor to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then looking at the second operation you describe at paragraph 33, you say that the MUP managed to enter Prilep. You say that three police officers were killed in Prilep. And then you go on to say that: "During this second operation, the MUP did not go to the Lake Radonjic area," you say, "that was not possible."
